results.summary: This design implements a ring oscillator whose frequency is measured by a 64-bit counter. The counter value is shifted by the cnt_shift inputs and can be stopped or reset via dedicated pins. The silicon test reports confirm operation, with the author measuring a ring oscillator frequency of approximately 504 MHz from the counter output. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout demo board.

The design chains 128 D flip-flops in series, creating a long shift register. The documentation is extremely sparse, stating only that it uses "magic mixed with stuff" and requires two "encabultors" for testing. No meaningful technical description, test procedure, or external hardware specification is provided. The project appears to be a joke or placeholder submission.

This design draws a bouncing ball on a 640x480 VGA display using a hardware physics engine. Commands to set position and velocity are received via SPI, and the ball rebounds off the screen edges. It requires a TinyVGA-style PMOD for video output and an SPI source for commands. The design was verified with a cocotb testbench and gate-level simulation.

This is an 8-bit processor that communicates with an external FPGA driver via SPI and can animate a 7-segment display. The driver initializes instruction and data memories from .mem files, then signals the processor to execute. The user can view register contents or watch an animation on the display after execution. The design requires an external FPGA (e.g., Digilent Nexys A7) and optionally an SPI device.

This project generates a 640x480 VGA demoscene-style image with an animated background and a central logo inspired by the Tiny Tapeout mark. The image is computed entirely in combinational logic without any frame buffer or external memory, resulting in a pixelated retro look. It requires a VGA PMOD for output and offers optional controls to invert colors or freeze the logo. The design is simple and synthesizable, suitable for education and demonstration.

This circuit implements a 4-bit password security system using combinational logic and an SR latch. Entering the correct code lights a green LED, while the trap code (1111) triggers a persistent alarm with a buzzer and red LED that requires manual reset. It is designed for simulation in Wokwi using a DIP switch, push buttons, LEDs, and a buzzer. The project demonstrates basic combinational and sequential logic for hardware security.

This design implements a 1D Kalman filter that fuses accelerometer and gyroscope data from an MPU-6500 IMU to compute Roll and Pitch angles. It uses an SPI master to read the sensor, a CORDIC core for atan2, and outputs the angles via UART at 9600 baud. External hardware required includes an MPU-6500 (or compatible) IMU and a USB-serial adapter for receiving data. The project is intended for FPGA-based sensor fusion and robotics applications.

This is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x32 grid, with support for both demo and manual modes. The grid can be displayed on a MAX7219 LED matrix (FC-16 module) or read directly via outputs. Multiple silicon testers confirmed it works, noting a minor bug causing a delay before the demo animation starts. External hardware required is a MAX7219 LED matrix module.

This design is an 8-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates a pseudo-random sequence. All input and bidirectional pins are unused, and the 8-bit output is available on the output pins. The documentation is minimal, providing no details on the polynomial or test results. It appears to be a simple educational or test circuit.

This project claims to implement a digital OTA (operational transconductance amplifier) using a 50 kHz clock and two input signals. The documentation is very sparse, stating only that the output current is proportional to the number of pulses in the output stages. No external hardware is specified, and no test results are provided. The design appears to be a placeholder or incomplete submission.
